basis.text: Duncan's history of the 1910s ('It was opened on July 22nd') and the nurse Sallie Myers in 1909 (quoted by a Park Service seminar paper of 2010) give 22 July without a source; the 1863 telegrams and letters bracket it (site chosen Jul 14, hospital tents arrived at the depot Jul 15, still 'being established' Jul 24, earliest dated transfers found Jul 24). No writing found gives 20 July.

default.label: Jul 22: the camp opens for patients (the earliest dated transfers found are Jul 24)

animation.note: The camp stands as tents from about Jul 15 (Janes's site chosen on Jul 14; hospital tents arrived at the depot on Jul 15) and is shown receiving patients from Jul 22; the earliest dated transfers found into it are Jul 24 and the corps hospitals empty into it through about Jul 29. Jul 20 has no source and stays selectable; the picture does not show patients earlier than Jul 22.

default.note: A medical history of the 1910s and a nurse's article of 1909 each say Jul 22 without a source; the papers of 1863 only bracket the opening. Opening for patients, completion of the tents and the first transfers are different days.

positions.label: Jul 22: a medical history of the 1910s and a nurse's article of 1909; the 1863 record fits it

support.page_note: printed page not read; the sentence stands in the chapter Gettysburg (chapter VII), under the paragraph on the hospital east of the town beside the York Pike; the reprint is undated (catalogued 191-?; the written date is the latest it can be: the Surgeon General's office letter of 19 Oct 1916 describes the bound reprints, and the text cites a source of 1911)
support.quote: It was opened on July 22nd and not closed until November 20, 1863

witness.name: Louis C. Duncan
witness.role: Captain, Medical Corps, US Army; medical historian, writing decades after the war (not a witness)

support.note: A history of the 1910s, which says 'It was opened on July 22nd' in plain words and gives no source. The same sentence gives Nov 20 for the close; it names no document. It is the 'early medical historian' of the Park Service paper of 2010.

support.quote: people took the soldiers into their houses and cared for them until Camp Letterman, the hospital camp, was opened on July 22

witness.name: Sally (Sallie) Myers
witness.role: Gettysburg schoolteacher and nurse in July 1863, later at Camp Letterman; quoted from her article 'Gettysburg's Memories of its Terrible Fourth', North American, 4 Jul 1909

support.note: The Park Service paper (2010) reports this passage from a source it names; the original was not read for this research, so the citation stands on the paper, which prints it. A reminiscence of forty-six years; it says 'opened' and gives the day, with no source. The paper says Myers 'also noted' it, so the two dates (Duncan and Myers) are two writers who each say 22 July; whether Duncan drew on Myers or the reverse is not shown.

support.quote: orders to move the patients in the 1st Corps hospitals were received on July 22

witness.name: William F. Norris
witness.role: Surgeon at a Gettysburg hospital (the Park Service paper places him with the First Corps hospitals); letters of July 1863 in the Park Service vertical files, quoted by the Park Service paper

support.note: The Park Service paper (2010) reports this passage from a source it names; the original was not read for this research, so the citation stands on the paper, which prints it. The paper puts the orders at 22 July and says the move took place the next day and at the end of the week; Norris writes on 26 July that his hospital moved to the General Hospital that day. The sentence is the paper's summary, not Norris's own words; it says that move orders came on 22 July, not that the camp opened then.

support.quote: soon all those who are not able to be moved far will be carried to the general hospital that is being established here

witness.name: William C. Way
witness.role: Chaplain, 24th Michigan Infantry; letter of 24 Jul 1863 printed in the Detroit Advertiser and Tribune of 30 Jul 1863, quoted by the Park Service paper

support.note: The Park Service paper (2010) reports this passage from a source it names; the original was not read for this research, so the citation stands on the paper, which prints it. On 24 July the general hospital 'is being established': not yet complete, and the transfers had not begun in numbers. This sets the earliest the camp could be called open as about 22 to 24 July and does not date the opening by itself. The newspaper itself was not read.

support.quote: Have selected a fine site for the camp. Am anxiously awaiting the tents

witness.name: Henry Janes
witness.role: Surgeon, US Volunteers, in charge of the hospitals at Gettysburg

support.note: Telegram of 14 Jul 1863 from Gettysburg to Washington: the site is chosen and the tents have not come. The camp does not exist as a hospital on 14 Jul; this is a lower bound, not an opening. The sentence before it, on the 9th, is the same Janes: 'I shall be able to begin the permanent hospital soon, if I can get the hospital tents'.

support.quote: The hospital tents arrived to-day, and are being put up

witness.name: W. G. Rankin
witness.role: Captain and depot quartermaster at Gettysburg; telegram to Colonel Ingalls, 15 Jul 1863

support.note: A quartermaster's telegram about his depot: he does not say the tents are for the general hospital or where they are being put up; read with Janes's telegram of the day before ('awaiting the tents'), it is the likeliest meaning but it is an inference, not a statement. It puts the tents on the ground from 15 Jul, a week before 22 Jul.

support.page_note: printed page not read in the text layer; the case stands in the chapter on wounds of the spine
support.quote: He was treated in the field hospital until July 24th, when lie was sent to Camp Letterman Hospital

witness.name: Surgeon General's Office (case history of Private Luther Weaver, 126th New York; reported by Acting Assistant Surgeon H. H. Dutton)
witness.role: Case history in the Medical and Surgical History, Part I vol. II (1870), compiled from the surgeons' reports

support.note: One of three cases that name a transfer to Camp Letterman on 24 Jul (a second says 'transfen-ed to Camp Letterman on July 24th'; a third 27 Jul). Two other cases name 'Camp Letterman Hospital' for 6 Jul and for the day after a wound of 2 Jul: that cannot be literal (Janes was still awaiting tents on 14 Jul) and is read as the later name of the general hospital applied to whatever hospital held the man first. These cases show the camp receiving men by 24 Jul; they do not say it was the first day.

support.page_note: printed page 62 read from the running head 'LEAVES FROM THE' in the text; the letter is headed 'Gettysburg, July 27, 1863. Wednesday evening': 27 July 1863 was a Monday and the entry before it is 'Tuesday, 28th', so the date is taken as 29 July at the latest in the book's own order; the heading is inconsistent
support.quote: The Third and Fifth Corps are being brought into the General Hospital, which is near the railroad

witness.name: Emily B. Souder
witness.role: Nurse (Philadelphia volunteer) with the Second Corps hospital at Gettysburg; letter to her husband

support.note: The corps hospitals are being merged into the General Hospital within the week of 22 to 29 July. It does not give an opening day. The Park Service paper dates this passage 27 July from the printed heading.

support.page_note: printed page 80 read from the running head 'UNITED STATES CHRISTIAN COMMISSION' that stands in the paragraph before the passage
support.quote: July 28th, about the time of our removal to the General Hospital

witness.name: United States Christian Commission, Philadelphia office (annual report for 1863)
witness.role: Report of the Commission's work at Gettysburg, printed 1864

support.note: By 28 July the Commission moved its tents to the General Hospital, so the camp was running; it says 'about the time'.

inference.step: Two later writers say the camp 'was opened on July 22' (Duncan, in the 1910s, and Myers, in 1909, the latter as printed by a Park Service paper), and neither gives a source. The 1863 papers do not state an opening but bracket it: the site was chosen and tents awaited on 14 Jul, the hospital tents arrived on 15 Jul, move orders for a corps hospital came on 22 Jul, the general hospital was still 'being established' on 24 Jul, the earliest dated transfers found into it are 24 Jul and the Christian Commission moved in about 28 Jul. 22 July sits inside that bracket; 20 July has no support.

weighing.summary: Two values: 20 July and 22 July. No writing found gives 20 July: the Park Service page that was reported for it could not be read as text (the word Letterman is not on the page as served) and the Trust page is not reachable. Two later writers say the camp 'was opened on July 22' (a medical history of the 1910s and a nurse in 1909, as printed by a Park Service paper of 2010 that calls the exact date 'hard to ascertain'); neither gives a source. The papers of 1863 do not state the opening but bracket it: the site was chosen and tents awaited on 14 Jul, tents arrived on 15 Jul, orders to move a corps hospital came on 22 Jul, the general hospital was still 'being established' on 24 Jul, the earliest dated transfers found are 24 Jul and the corps hospitals were merging into it by about 29 Jul. 22 July fits and 20 July has nothing; the opening day itself is not stated by a writer of the time, so the default is inferred, weighted.
weighing.who: Duncan was a medical officer and historian, not a witness. Myers was a Gettysburg teacher who nursed in the town hospitals and at the camp: present, but writing in 1909. Norris (First Corps hospital surgeon), Way (chaplain of the 24th Michigan) and Souder (a nurse of the Second Corps hospital) were on the spot; Janes, who chose the site and ran the hospitals, and Rankin, the depot quartermaster, were the men who dealt with the tents. None of them states the day the camp opened.
weighing.when: The 1863 witnesses wrote 14 Jul to 29 Jul, in the weeks of the establishing. The two writers who give 22 July wrote 46 years (Myers) and decades (Duncan, undated, 1910s) later. The rubric puts a contemporaneous letter or dispatch above a later history above a reminiscence; here the contemporaneous writings do not state the value, so the later ones are the only writers who give a day. They are weighed as a marker, not as a document: the tier is inferred, not documented.
weighing.where: Janes, Rankin and Norris were at Gettysburg and wrote what they dealt with; Way and Souder were with hospitals that were being merged into the camp. The 22 July orders are for a First Corps hospital to move, which fits a camp ready to take men; they do not say the camp had opened that day. The earliest dated transfers found, of 24 July, were a move of men already in hospital: opening for patients, finishing the tents and the first transfers are different days, and 22 July is the opening for patients as the two later writers give it.
weighing.how_knew: Janes and Rankin report what they did and received. Norris, Way and Souder saw the moves. Myers and Duncan do not say how they knew; the Park Service paper reports their sentences without saying where Duncan or Myers got the date. Neither the Trust, Wikipedia nor the Park Service ranger page could be read, so the sources behind 20 July are not known.
weighing.clock: A date, not an hour; no clock correction applies. All the writers use the civil calendar of 1863. The Souder letter heading ('July 27 ... Wednesday evening') is inconsistent with the calendar; the entry before it is dated Tuesday the 28th, so it is read as 29 July.
weighing.independence: Duncan and Myers are two writers but not shown to be independent (Duncan gives no source; Myers wrote in 1909 and may have drawn on the common memory of the town). The Park Service paper (2010) cites both and adds nothing to them. The papers of 1863 are independent of each other (Janes, Rankin, Norris, Way, Souder, the Christian Commission, the case histories) but none states the opening, so they test the date rather than carry it. The rest of the value (Jul 20) has no writer. The default therefore has two groups saying 22 July and several that fit; it carries the flag for later writers only.

source_panel_text: Jul 22: a medical history of the 1910s and a Gettysburg nurse in 1909 each say the camp opened on July 22; the 1863 telegrams and letters fit it (hospital tents arrived Jul 15, camp still 'being established' Jul 24). No writing found gives Jul 20. The other value is listed.

what_would_change_it: A source behind the plan's 20 July (the Trust page, the ranger page or a Wikipedia source) that states 20 July in a text of 1863 would move the default. A writing of 1863 that says the general hospital 'was opened', 'opened' or 'received its first patients' on a named day (Janes's report to Letterman, a Sanitary or Christian Commission diary, the Detroit paper of 30 Jul 1863, the Norris letters, the Myers article of 1909) would replace the later writers' 22 July with a documented value.
